Triggers.value: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Threat.value: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

issues.item: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other selected items describe fear-based reactivity, hypervigilance, sexual trauma triggers, and intrusive/reliving memory phenomena after rape. In that context, prominent risk-taking pulls in the opposite direction of the otherwise avoidance/vigilance-focused presentation and is not supported by appraisals or maladaptive-strategy items. This creates a within-node and cross-node coherence problem.

vignette:
Rekha is a 61-year-old married woman who works long days as an agricultural laborer in California’s Central Valley. She came to therapy at the urging of her daughter, who had grown alarmed by how withdrawn and jumpy her mother had become. For Rekha, the trouble began three years ago, when she was walking home along a dusty irrigation ditch after a late shift. A man she vaguely recognized from a neighboring camp emerged from behind a stand of eucalyptus trees. He had a dog with him—a lean, barking animal that lunged at her legs while the man forced her to the ground. She remembers the dog’s hot breath on her skin, the man’s weight, the gravel digging into her back, and the feeling of being utterly unable to move or scream. The assault lasted perhaps fifteen minutes, but in her memory it has no end. She has never told her husband what happened; she is certain he would blame her for walking alone, and she has come to believe that she should have known better, should have sensed the danger before it arrived.

In the months that followed, Rekha’s life began to shrink. She now avoids the path where it happened, taking a longer route that adds half an hour to her walk home. But the memory is not confined to that place. Several times a week, something in her surroundings—the bark of a neighbor’s dog, the sight of a man’s boots, the pressure of her husband’s hand on her shoulder as she cooks—instantly brings the full event back to her, and she feels as though she is lying on that gravel again, the dog snarling, the man’s weight pressing her down. The memories are like a film that plays over and over, always the same, always unwelcome. She has learned to recognize the moments just before they arrive: a sudden coldness in her chest, a ringing in her ears, her body reacting before her mind has even had time to think. What frightens her most is that she cannot stop it. She has tried to push the images away, to focus on her work, but the memory seems to have its own timing.

Her sleep has become a battlefield. She lies awake for hours, listening to the wind in the trees, the creak of the house, the distant barking of dogs. She has difficulty falling asleep because she needs to stay alert, certain that if she lets her guard down, something will happen again. When her husband reaches for her in the night, she stiffens and pulls away. She has come to dread any sexual situation or intimacy, because the moment his hands touch her, her body floods with alarm as though the assault is starting all over again. She reacts with a sharp gasp or a flinch when he touches her unexpectedly, and she has seen the hurt in his eyes, but she cannot explain it. She has told herself that she is broken, that her body no longer belongs to her.

At work, the consequences have been concrete. She used to be one of the fastest pickers in her crew, but now she startles at every unexpected sound—a dog barking in the distance, a supervisor approaching from behind. She has started working at the far end of the rows, away from the others, because she cannot bear the feeling of being surrounded. Her supervisor has noticed her slower pace and has spoken to her twice about it. She is terrified of losing her job, but she is equally terrified of explaining why she cannot concentrate.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment two weeks ago, when her granddaughter ran up to embrace her and Rekha shoved the child away without thinking, her heart pounding, the dog’s bark echoing in her ears. Her daughter wept and demanded to know what was wrong. Rekha sat in her kitchen afterward, staring at her own trembling hands, and realized she could no longer keep the memory sealed away. She is afraid of what will happen if she speaks about it—afraid her husband will leave her, afraid she will be seen as dirty or weak—but she is even more afraid of the next time the film starts playing and she cannot make it stop. She hopes, more than anything, to find a way to sleep through the night without watching the door.
